name: Hana Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana, I'm 27, and I supervise the accounts payable team at the head office of a big biscuit and snack maker. Accounts payable means we pay the suppliers: the flour mill, the packaging firm, the haulage companies. There are six of us in the team, and the factory is right behind our office, so the whole building smells of baking. I live with my partner Sam, who's in the third year of an electrician apprenticeship.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get in at half eight, check the payment run, and sort out whatever invoices don't match the orders. That's most of the job really, chasing why the flour mill billed us for twenty tonnes when the factory says it got eighteen. I like it when the numbers finally line up. What wears me out is month end, when everyone wants everything paid yesterday and the system freezes twice a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief, and leave it there. I'm not one for big opinions online. At work I'd probably say we should just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even the small stuff would worry me, because matching invoices is exactly the routine work a tool could pick up. Two years ago they moved payroll to a service centre in another city, and that wasn't AI, just cost cutting. We've got less than a month saved, and Sam's apprentice wage is about half of mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, but I'd keep my eyes open. I'd ask my manager straight out whether accounts payable is next on the list for the service centre. And I'd stop buying lunch from the canteen, which would save about forty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit on edge. It's not the AI. The company is always looking for the next team to move, and accounts payable could be it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I just don't trust what I can't check. If a program tells me an invoice matches, I'd still want to look at it myself. My friend Leanne uses them for everything, and she sent a supplier the wrong payment because of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if your team did move to the service centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have nothing nearby, honestly. There are maybe two other big offices in our city, and one is a bank that's closing branches. I'd be looking at shop work or the factory floor.

say: I'd say it's a **relief** and leave it there.
At work I'd tell people to **get on with it**, without big opinions.
think: **Invoice matching** is exactly the routine work a small tool could take.
Payroll already **moved away** to cut costs, so my team could be next.
do: Ask my manager **straight out** if accounts payable is moving next.
Stop buying **canteen lunches** to save about forty a month.
Carry on working while **watching** for signs of change.
feel: **On edge**, because the company is always looking to move a team.
S0.quote: The company is always looking for the next team to move, and accounts payable could be it.
fieldNote: Her worry predates AI: **payroll was moved** two years ago.
She refuses AI tools because she **can't check** what they do.
**Few local office jobs** turn a small change into a big risk.

steps.text: Ask her manager whether accounts payable is moving to the service centre
Bring lunch from home instead of buying it in the canteen
Keep matching invoices and running payments as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for some things, but someone still has to check. In the team I'd tell everyone not to panic until we hear something official. Online I'd say nothing, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my team goes from six to two, and they keep the cheapest two. Checking and buying are both on that card, and that's our whole day. I'd probably be told to train the new system and then be thanked for my service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking for a way onto the factory side, maybe as a shift supervisor, because that's hands-on and slower to change. I'd ask Sam to finish his apprenticeship fast and get qualified, because his wage would matter more. And I'd go back to living very cheaply, no holidays, no takeaways, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach, if I'm honest. I'm not good with new systems, and I'd be learning one just to be replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to the factory. Do you know anything about production?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, but I know the people, I've paid their suppliers for five years. The factory always needs shift supervisors for nights. It's less pay than I'd like, but at least nobody's replacing a person who stops the line when the dough's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI system if the company asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, but I'd do the bare minimum. I'd check every single thing it did, which would probably drive my manager mad. I'd rather be slow and right.

say: The tools make sense for some things, but someone **still has to check**.
I'd tell my team **not to panic** until there's official news.
think: My team probably shrinks **from six to two**, keeping the cheapest.
**Checking and buying** are on the card, and that's our whole day.
do: Look for a **shift supervisor** job on the factory floor.
Push Sam to **qualify** as an electrician quickly.
Cut spending to **the bone**: no holidays, no takeaways.
feel: **Sick** at learning a system just to be replaced by it.
S1.quote: Nobody's replacing a person who stops the line when the dough's wrong.
fieldNote: She picks the **factory floor** as her escape, knowing it's hands-on.
Sam's **apprenticeship** becomes the household's safety net.
She'd learn the system only **reluctantly**, and check everything twice.

steps.text: Apply for a night shift supervisor role in the factory
Cut out holidays and takeaways completely
Learn the new AI payment system, but check every match by hand
Help Sam finish his electrician qualification early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and somebody in charge should have seen it coming. I'd say it in the office and at home. I'm not a protester, but I'd vote for whoever promised to slow it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's gone. The whole finance office would be gone, not just my team. Sam's electrician work is hands-on, so it's the only thing in our house that lasts until the robots around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd try to get onto the factory floor, before everyone else in the office has the same idea. I'd save every penny, maybe a hundred and fifty a month if we stopped going out completely. If it all went at once, I'd ask my mum and dad if we could move back with them, though their house is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I don't have a plan, I have a list of fallbacks, and none of them are great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between a plan and a list of fallbacks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plan is when you know where you're going. A list of fallbacks is factory, mum and dad, shop work, in that order. I'd be grabbing at the first one that came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Sam talk about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would say don't worry, I'll look after us, and I'd love him for it. But an apprentice wage doesn't cover rent for two. Sam qualifies next year, which helps, but robots come for electricians too, just three years later.

say: It's **too fast**, and someone in charge should have seen it.
I'd **vote** for whoever promised to slow it down.
think: The **whole finance office** goes, not just my team.
Sam's **electrician work** is our only income lasting until robots.
do: Rush to get a **factory floor** job before others do.
Save about **a hundred and fifty** a month by stopping all outings.
Ask my parents if we could **move back** with them.
feel: **Frightened**, with fallbacks but no real plan.
S2.quote: A plan is when you know where you're going. A list of fallbacks is factory, mum and dad, shop work, in that order.
fieldNote: She draws a sharp line between a **plan** and **fallbacks**.
Her partner's **trade** is the household's lifeline, with three years' grace.
Not a protester, she'd use her **vote** instead.

steps.text: Apply for a factory floor job before the office cuts start
Save a hundred and fifty a month by stopping outings
Ask her parents about moving back into their small house
Vote for candidates promising to slow AI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. People could get ready if they're told honestly. I'd probably say that to my manager in my appraisal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know myself, I wouldn't change until I had to. But five years is long enough that even I'd see it coming. I'd still assume finance is gone by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get onto the factory side within two years, while there's still a choice of shifts. I'd try to build up two months of savings by 2029, using whatever Sam earns once he's qualified. We'd probably put off getting a mortgage, even though that's what we'd been saving toward, sort of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less shaky. Five years feels like knowing the redundancy letter is coming in five years instead of next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the mortgage. What would putting it off mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means renting longer, which we hate, because the landlord never fixes anything. But a mortgage on two wobbly incomes would be mad. We'd wait until we know Sam's work and mine are settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your team in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to start thinking about where else they could go now, while they've got a wage. I'm not good at the inspirational stuff. I'd just be straight with them.

say: Five years is **something**, if people are told honestly.
I'd raise it with my manager at my **appraisal**.
think: I **wouldn't change** until I had to, but I'd see it coming.
do: Move to the **factory side** within two years.
Build **two months** of savings by 2029 using Sam's qualified wage.
Put off the **mortgage** until both incomes feel settled.
feel: **Worried but less shaky**, like seeing a letter coming in advance.
S3.quote: Five years feels like knowing the redundancy letter is coming in five years instead of next week.
fieldNote: She is honest that she **resists change** until forced.
Delaying the **mortgage** is a real cost she accepts calmly.
She'd be **straight** with her team rather than inspiring them.

steps.text: Move to a factory floor role within two years
Build two months of savings by 2029
Postpone buying a home until both jobs settle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for people being caught out. I'd say it fairly firmly at work, because most of the office would still be ignoring it. I'm practical like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough that I'd probably drift for the first five. But I'd be 37 and maybe have kids by then, which changes everything. I'd want to be somewhere safer before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in accounts payable a few more years, then move into production planning or a supervisor role at the factory. I'd do one of the company's food safety courses, because that's needed on the floor and nobody wants to do it. Savings would go up slowly, maybe fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. Ten years feels like real life rather than a cliff edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drift for five years. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I know I'm slow to move, it's just how I am. Having Sam nagging me would help, Sam's always the one who pushes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the company to do with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell people which jobs are going and when, and let them try other jobs inside the company first. Most of my team would happily move to the factory or the warehouse if someone just asked.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, so nobody should be caught out.
I'd say it **firmly at work**, because most people would ignore it.
think: I'd probably **drift** for the first five years.
By 37 I might have **kids**, so I'd want to be safer first.
do: Stay in accounts payable a few years, then move to **factory supervision**.
Take a **food safety course** that the factory floor needs.
Raise savings slowly, about **fifty a month**.
feel: **Mostly okay**, like real life rather than a cliff edge.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like real life rather than a cliff edge.
fieldNote: She expects to **drift** and relies on Sam to push her.
She'd want the company to offer **internal moves** first.
Even with time, she still expects her **finance job** to go.

steps.text: Take the company's food safety course
Move into factory supervision within five years
Save fifty a month into a separate account

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My job is all invoices and checking, and we've got less than a month of savings. What would help is the company being honest about what's going, and letting people move into the factory first before they hire from outside.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. My partner Sam's apprenticeship is the only reason I'm not more scared, and lots of people don't have that.

headlineQuote: My partner Sam's apprenticeship is the only reason I'm not more scared, and lots of people don't have that.
portrait: Hana is 27 and supervises **six accounts payable** clerks at a biscuit and snack maker's head office.
She lives with Sam, an **apprentice electrician**, and they have under a month saved.
She never uses AI, because she **can't check** what it does.
She sees the **factory floor** as her safest move, because hands-on work lasts longer.
She is **anxious or alarmed** in every picture, and admits she resists change until forced.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her checking job goes fast and savings are thin.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest notice** of which office jobs are going.
First chance at **factory jobs** for existing office staff.
